entry: Perennial river in Northeast Asia, the border between the Russian Far East and northeastern [[China]]. The Amur proper is 2,824 km (1,755 mi) long, and its [[Drainage basin|drainage basin]] covers 1,855,000 sq km (716,000 sq mi). Including its main tributary, the Argun, the river is 4,444 km (2,761 mi) long, the world's tenth longest river. It rises where the Shilka and Argun meet at 303 m (994 ft) and is joined at Tongjiang by the Songhua. Near Khabarovsk the Ussuri joins, and the river turns north and then east to an [[Estuary|estuary]] at Nikolayevsk-on-Amur, about 20 km (12 mi) upstream of its mouth on the Strait of Tartary. The river holds large predatory fish and several species of [[Trout|trout]]. The kaluga, one of the world's largest freshwater fish, is a [[Sturgeon|sturgeon]] reaching 5.6 m (18 ft). Under the Treaty of Aigun (1858), territory north of the river passed to [[Russia]].

Stationary park offering rides, games and entertainment events. Unlike temporary funfairs and carnivals, amusement parks are built for long-lasting operation and cater to several age groups. A theme park is a type of amusement park built around a central theme. Amusement parks evolved from European fairs, pleasure gardens and picnic areas, and were also influenced by [[World's fair|world's fairs]]. Bakken in Klampenborg, [[Denmark]], Wurstelprater in [[Vienna]], and Tivoli Gardens in [[Copenhagen]] are the three oldest operating amusement parks in the world. Lake Compounce, opened in 1846, is considered the oldest continuously operating amusement park in [[North America]]. Mechanical rides developed in the 1860s and 1870s, and the [[Working class|working classes]] increasingly spent their wages on entertainment. After World War II, theme parks such as [[Disneyland]], which opened in 1955, integrated rides into cohesive narratives.

American actress known for both comedic and dramatic roles. She has been featured three times in annual rankings of the world's highest-paid actresses and has received six [[Academy Awards]] nominations, beginning with the independent comedy-drama *Junebug* (2005). She has won two Golden Globes. Her films include *Doubt* (2008), *The Fighter* (2010), *American Hustle* (2013) and *Arrival* (2016). In 2014, [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named her one of the 100 most influential people in the world.

American singer-songwriter who began in contemporary Christian music (CCM) before crossing over to [[Pop music|pop]]. In 1986 she scored her first Billboard Hot 100 no. 1 song, a duet with Peter Cetera, “The Next Time I Fall.” Her album *Heart in Motion* (1991) was her best-selling, selling five million copies in the U.S. As of 2009 she had sold more than 30 million albums worldwide and won six [[Grammy Awards]]. She received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2006.

American actress, comedian and podcaster. She began in improvisational theater at [[Chicago|Chicago]]'s Second City and co-founded the Upright Citizens Brigade Theatre in [[New York City]]. She joined [[Saturday Night Live]] in 2001 and starred as Leslie Knope in the sitcom *Parks and Recreation* (2009–2015), for which she won a Golden Globe Award. She co-hosted the Golden Globe Awards with [[Tina Fey]] four times. Poehler has voiced characters in the [[Pixar]] film *Inside Out* franchise.

British singer and songwriter known for her distinctive contralto voice and for blending soul, [[Jazz|jazz]] and [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]]. Her second album, *Back to Black* (2006), was an international success and one of the best-selling albums of all time. At the 50th [[Grammy Awards]] in 2008 she won five, becoming the first British woman to do so. Her career was often overshadowed by substance abuse, mental illness and addiction, culminating in her death from alcohol poisoning.

[[Civil war]] in China (755–763) against [[Tang dynasty|Tang]] rule. It began on December 16, 755, when An Lushan, military governor of the [[Taiyuan]] Commandery, marched his army out of Fanyang. Rebels captured the imperial capital Chang'an after Emperor Xuanzong fled to [[Sichuan]], and they proclaimed the short-lived Yan dynasty. An Lushan was assassinated by his son, and rebel leadership passed to Shi Siming and then to Shi Chaoyi. Divisions among the rebels and counterattacks by Tang forces and their allies brought the Yan dynasty's fall in 763. The war caused famine, displacement and destruction, and the Tang permanently lost the Western Regions. Regional military governors gained autonomy, and their secessionism continued into the [[Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period]]. The later [[Song dynasty]] distrusted prominent commanders to avoid a repeat, and the rebellion began the long decline of the Guanzhong region.

Christian movement of the 16th-century Radical Reformation. Anabaptists hold that [[Baptism|baptism]] is valid only when a believer freely confesses faith, and they reject infant baptism. Their Schleitheim Confession (1527) set out foundational beliefs; its author, Michael Sattler, was arrested and executed shortly afterward. Protestant state churches and Roman Catholics persecuted them. The [[Amish]], [[Mennonites]] and Hutterites descend from the early movement. Most Anabaptists reject violence and oaths and take no part in civil government.

Genus of large, semiaquatic [[Boidae|boas]] (*Eunectes*) found in tropical [[South America]]. The name *Eunectes* means “good swimmer” in Greek. Two to four living species and one extinct species are recognized. The green anaconda (*Eunectes murinus*) is the largest snake in the world by weight and is second in length only to the [[Reticulated python]]. Anacondas range from Ecuador, Brazil and Colombia to Venezuela and northern Argentina.

City (pop., 2020: 346,824) in northern Orange County, California, part of the Greater Los Angeles area. Anaheim is the most populous city in Orange County and is home to the [[Disneyland]] Resort. The city remained largely agricultural until Disneyland opened on July 17, 1955, after which hotels and residential districts followed. It is also home to the Anaheim Ducks of the [[National Hockey League]] and the Los Angeles Angels of [[Major League Baseball]].

Sexual activity involving penetration of the anus or rectum, most commonly by the penis. Other forms include anal fingering, the use of sex toys, [[Anilingus|anilingus]] and pegging. Anal sex is commonly associated with male homosexuality, but not all homosexual men engage in it, and it is not uncommon in heterosexual relationships. Pleasure may come from stimulation of nerve endings in the anal region. Orgasm may result from indirect stimulation of the [[Prostate|prostate]] in men, or of the [[Clitoris|clitoris]] or an area of the vagina (sometimes called the [[G-spot|G-spot]]) in women. The anal and rectal tissue are delicate and does not lubricate like the vagina, so anal sex can facilitate the spread of [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]]. Without a [[Condom|condom]], it is considered the riskiest form of sexual activity, and the [[World Health Organization]] recommends safe-sex practices. In some countries it is a criminal offense punishable by corporal or [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]].

Ancient Chinese philosophical text of sayings attributed to [[Confucius]] and his contemporaries, traditionally believed to have been compiled by his followers. Scholars consider large portions of *The Analects* to have been composed during the Warring States period (475–221 BCE), and the work reached its final form during the mid-[[Han dynasty]] (206 BCE–220 CE). In the late [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279 CE) it was ranked above the older Five Classics as one of the “Four Books.” Confucius held that a ruler's virtue (*de*) was the prerequisite for leadership, and that cultivating *ren* (benevolence), beginning with filial piety, and *li* (ritual propriety) produced ethically cultivated people. The text is a central work of [[Confucianism|Confucianism]] and has been among China's most widely read books for more than two millennia.

Drug used to relieve pain, also called a painkiller or pain reliever. Analgesics are distinct from [[Anesthesia|anesthetics]], which temporarily reduce mobility, although some drugs have both effects. Aspirin, [[Ibuprofen]], naproxen and diclofenac are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) that reduce pain and fever and, in higher doses, inflammation. [[Paracetamol|Paracetamol]] (acetaminophen) treats mild to moderate pain and fever, with effects lasting two to four hours, and is generally safe at recommended doses. [[Opioid|Opioids]] such as [[Morphine]] act on the opioid receptor system and carry risks of overdose, misuse and [[Addiction]]. COX-2 inhibitors, developed to spare the gut, were found to increase the risk of cardiovascular events by 40% on average, and rofecoxib and valdecoxib were withdrawn. Many NSAIDs are sold over the counter, while stronger analgesics are prescription drugs.

Family of statistical methods for comparing the means of two or more groups by analyzing [[Variance|variance]]. The method compares variation between group means with variation within each group, using an F-test. If between-group variation is substantially larger, the group means are likely different. It rests on the law of total variance and generalizes the t-test beyond two means. It was developed by the statistician [[Ronald Fisher]], whose 1925 book *Statistical Methods for Research Workers* made it widely known.

Study of geometry using a coordinate system, also called coordinate or Cartesian geometry. It usually applies the [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinate system]] to equations for planes, straight lines and circles, mostly in two dimensions. It is used in physics, engineering, aviation, statistics and economics, and it underlies most modern geometry. Apollonius of Perga's *Conics* used reference lines similar to a modern coordinate frame. The 11th-century Persian mathematician [[Omar Khayyam]] laid down principles of the subject in his *Treatise on Demonstrations of Problems of Algebra* (1070). It was independently invented by [[René Descartes]] and [[Pierre de Fermat]] in the 17th century, although Descartes is sometimes given sole credit. Descartes's essay *La Géométrie* appeared in 1637.

Branch of [[Number theory|number theory]] that uses methods from mathematical analysis to study the integers. It is often said to have begun with [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]]'s 1837 introduction of Dirichlet L-functions, which he used to prove Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions. Multiplicative number theory studies the distribution of [[Prime number|primes]], including the [[Prime number theorem]], which states that the number of primes up to x is approximately x / ln(x). Additive number theory concerns the additive structure of the integers, such as [[Goldbach's conjecture]] that every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. Bernhard Riemann's 1859 memoir on the [[Riemann zeta function]] led to the unproven [[Riemann hypothesis]], which concerns its zeros.

Broad school of thought in contemporary Western philosophy, especially anglophone philosophy. It emphasizes analysis, clear prose, rigorous argument, formal logic and the natural sciences, and is characterized by the linguistic turn, a concern with language and meaning. It is often contrasted with continental philosophy, such as [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]]. The tradition proliferated from around the turn of the 20th century. Central figures include [[Gottlob Frege]], [[Bertrand Russell]], G. E. Moore and [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]]. W. V. O. Quine, Saul Kripke and others led a decline of logical positivism and a revival of metaphysics, and the school developed the philosophy of language, mathematics and science.

Psychological practices of [[Carl Jung]], also called Jungian analysis. The term was designed to distinguish Jung's work from [[Sigmund Freud|Freud]]'s psychoanalysis as their seven-year collaboration ended in 1912–1913. It began as a theory of psychological complexes in the “Zurich school” at the Burghölzli hospital in [[Zurich]]. Jung later turned it into a method for investigating archetypes and the unconscious, and into a specialized psychotherapy. Key concepts include anima and animus, the collective unconscious, individuation, the Self and the shadow. The Myers–Briggs Type Indicator is loosely based on Jung's theories of psychological types, including [[Extraversion and introversion|extraversion and introversion]]. His long collaboration with [[Wolfgang Pauli]] reflected his commitment to science.

Trickster figure of Akan folklore from southern [[Ghana]], usually depicted as a spider. His name means “spider” in the Akan language, and he is known for cunning, wit and trickery. He often outsmarts more powerful opponents and is both protagonist and antagonist in stories. Anansi was seen as synonymous with skill and [[Wisdom|wisdom]] in speech, and his tales were part of an exclusively [[Oral tradition|oral tradition]]. Spider tales are found throughout West Africa, and the Ghanaian tales are seen as their origin. Through the [[Atlantic slave trade]] they reached the [[Caribbean]], later spreading to [[Suriname]], [[Sierra Leone]], [[Curaçao]], Aruba and Bonaire. Ghanaian children are raised on the whole tradition, called *anansesem*, or spider tales.

Peninsula of West Asia that makes up most of the land area of [[Turkey]]. Also called Asia Minor, it is bounded by the Mediterranean Sea to the south, the Aegean Sea to the west, the Sea of Marmara to the northwest and the Black Sea to the north. The Sea of Marmara links the Black Sea and the Aegean through the [[Bosporus]] and the [[Dardanelles]]. Farming spread into Anatolia from the adjacent [[Fertile Crescent]] and was followed by a major migration of Anatolian farmers into Europe about 9,000 years ago. From the late 11th century the [[Seljuk Empire]] began the Turkification of the region, which continued under the [[Ottoman Empire]] until its collapse after World War I. Between 1894 and 1924, millions of non-Turkic peoples and Christians were killed by Ottoman authorities or expelled, especially about two million Greeks and an estimated 1.5 million Armenians.

Burmese king and founder of the Pagan Empire (r. from 1044). He is considered the father of the Burmese nation. He unified the [[Irrawaddy River|Irrawaddy]] valley for the first time and placed the Shan States and Arakan under Pagan's suzerainty. He halted the advance of the [[Khmer Empire]] into the Tenasserim coast and the upper Menam valley. By building weirs, he turned arid land around Pagan into rice granaries for Upper Burma. His administrative system was followed by later kings until the dynasty fell in 1287. He embraced [[Theravada]] Buddhism, and the dynasty's success later made its growth possible in Lan Na, Siam, [[Lan Xang]] and Cambodia in the 13th and 14th centuries.

Ancient Native American culture of the Four Corners region of the U.S., the forerunners of today's Pueblo peoples. It spanned southeastern [[Utah]], northeastern [[Arizona]], northwestern [[New Mexico]] and southwestern [[Colorado]]. Its communities, linked across the Colorado Plateau, lived in pit houses, clan houses, grand pueblos and cliff dwellings. Their architecture reflected knowledge of celestial sciences, and the kiva, a ceremonial space, was central to community life. The current agreement places their emergence around the 12th century BCE. Three [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] in the U.S. are credited to the Pueblos. The older term Anasazi comes from a [[Navajo]] phrase meaning “enemy ancestors,” and many Pueblo peoples consider it derogatory.

City (pop., 2020: 291,247) in south-central [[Alaska]], the state's largest. Officially the Municipality of Anchorage, it holds nearly 40 percent of the state's population. It began as a tent city in 1915 during construction of the Alaska Railroad, was incorporated as a city in 1920, and merged with the Greater Anchorage Area Borough in 1975. The city won the All-America City Award four times, in 1956, 1965, 1984–85 and 2002.

Small, common forage fish of the family Engraulidae, found mostly in marine waters. More than 140 species in 16 genera occur in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, the [[Black Sea]] and the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. Several species enter [[Brackish water|brackish water]], and some in South America are restricted to fresh water. Anchovies are usually classified as oily fish and feed on [[Plankton]]. They have a blunt snout with a rostral organ believed to be electro-sensory, and adults range from 2 to 40 cm in length. The earliest true anchovy fossil is *Eoengraulis* from the early Eocene of Monte Bolca, Italy. Anchovies are rare in the fossil record, possibly because they inhabit nearshore waters where fossilization is unlikely.

[[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] city-state in present-day [[Tunisia]], later the center of a major western Mediterranean empire. Merchants from Tyre founded the settlement, and after the [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]] conquered Phoenicia in the 7th century BC, Carthage became independent of its eastern neighbors. Its navy supported a network of colonies and vassals, and by 300 BC it controlled northwestern Africa, southern and eastern Iberia, and the islands of [[Sicily]], Sardinia, Corsica, Malta and the [[Balearic Islands]]. Its government combined elements of democracy, oligarchy and republicanism. Carthage fought the [[Punic Wars]] with Rome from 264 to 146 BC, and [[Hannibal]] invaded Italy with war elephants. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC after the Third Punic War. Much of what is known about Carthage comes from Roman and Greek sources, many written during or after the wars.
